To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) thrombolytic agents reduce mortality, but the risk to benefit ratio of thrombolytis is lower in patients presenting late (beyond 12 hours after the onset of symptoms), in patients with a history of prior infarction or congestive heart failure, or in patients who are older than 70 years; (c) thrombolytics reduce the incidence of reinfarction and recurrent angina, but do not reduce the incidence of congestive heart failure

(1) thrombolytic treatment should be initiated in the prehospital phase in selected patients; (2) adjunctive treatment with a β-blocker and angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor should be considered in all patients with acute myocardial infraction; (3) early noninvasive testing should be performed to identify patients with early reocclusion after thrombolytic or angioplasty treatment;

thrombolytic treatment is effective in the majority of patients with acute myocardial infraction and that the risk to benefit ratio of thrombolytcs depends on the patient population and the time window for treatment.

the development of new thrombolytics with a higher efficacy, better safety and improved pharmacokinetics.
a more precise definition of the indications for thrombolysis in acute myocardial ischemia.
the identification and treatment of patients at high risk for reperfusion failure.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
thrombolysis remains the treatment of choice in patients with acute myocardial infraction and ST-segment elevation.
the optimal management of acute myocardial infraction remains elusive.
the optimal treatment strategy for acute myocardial infraction is still unknown.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
reperfusion intervention in the acute phase of myocardial infarctions is a safe and effective treatment, and that the optimal strategy for the individual patient is still a matter of debate.
reperfusion therapy in acute myocardial is still in a state of flux.
thrombolytic intervention should be offered to patients with acute myocardial infraction, who present within 12 hours after the onset of chest pain, with a high probability of coronary occlusion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, despite the impressive progress made in the past decade, there is still room for further improvement in our approach to patients with acute myocardial infraction.
the risk of reperfusion therapy is not uniform across patients, and that the risk of thrombolysis may be acceptable for many patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarctions.
